Ex-UK air cargo rates steady but drift upwards to Asia
By Helen Hill

LONDON, Oct 3 (Reuter) - Carriers operating out of London are continuing to resist any formal rates increases, which usually take place in the autumn, despite pressure from higher jet fuel prices, a Reuter survey shows.
There are however clear signs of an upward drift in current rates to Asia, industry sources said, a reflection of continuing strong import demand.

The market seems to be optimistic about prospects for the fourth quarter. Roger Blacklock of the British International Freight Association (BIFA) reported a "general upturn across the board in the air cargo market", with members reporting quite good results.

Carriers claim to be looking for stability in the market and this is largely reflected in air cargo rates which are generally steady, with no any dramatic movements expected in the next few weeks, the sources said.
Jet kerosene prices have risen 20 percent since Iraqi troops entered Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq at end-August.

In the Netherlands, KLM is considering rising its prices, but so far appears to be alone. A spokesman said the carrier has conducted a study which looked at the possibility of passing higher fuel costs to its customers. But he stressed that no firm decisions have been taken.
All of the carriers Reuters spoke to for its latest UK report said they would not be increasing rates on the back of the fuel price rises.

Rates to Asia are however showing signs of drifting upwards with 1.19 stg a kg per 100 kg quoted to Hong Kong from London compared to 1.18 previously and Singapore at 1.24 stg a kg up from 1.23 stg. Tokyo and Seoul are respectively two pence higher at 1.97 stg a kg and 1.85 stg

German carrier Lufthansa's UK marketing manager, Ruediger Helm, said that the carrier has implemented some small increases on October 1 to certain destinations. These include Japanese cities such as Tokyo and Osaka as well as Kathmandu.
But he stressed the increases were extremely moderate and were not as a direct impact of the situation in the Middle East. No other additional surcharges were been considered..

Intra-European express traffic, on the other hand, has been subject of a five percent rates increase, added Helm. Express business has been much better, especially overnight services to Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

Thai International's cargo manager, Mike Miller, said that the UK-Asia market is very strong at the moment and because of this cargo was being trucked from the UK to the Thai carrier's freighter aircraft on continental Europe in Frankfurt and Paris.

Another reason for the demand for cargo space has been healthy passenger loads which have put pressure on the space allocated for cargo. Yields too are fairly healthy and are showing signs of edging upwards, he added. Bangkok usually hovers around the 1.23 level per kg.
Miller added Thai is another carrier that will not be implementing increases this autumn. "Most of us are waiting for the winter to pass and give the market some breathing space."
But he added if demand continued at the present rate the situation is likely to be reviewed in February/March next year.

Thai will be flying direct from London to Bangkok every day from October 26. Previously three of the weekly flights went via New Delhi but this stopover is being dropped.There will be no problem in filing the extra 12 tonnes weekly capacited generated by the new flights, added Miller.
Rates to Australia have also firmed rising to an average of 2.07 stg a kg from 2.05 stg on September 18 and 2.03 stg a fortnight earlier.

Graham Chamberlain, UK cargo manager for Qantas, said London- Australia is experiencing very strong demand. The Australian economy has been fairly healthy, with a downturn in inflation and some reasonable wage rises which has led consumers to buy more, he commented.

However, there is a lot of interest in the Australia air cargo market and Qantas in not alone in being a little worried about the extra capacity that is set to flood into the market as Christmas approaches and the effect this will have on the rates.
Until now rates to the country ex-London have been steady. Qantas operates two Boeing 747 aircraft daily to the market.

A cargo spokeswoman for Garuda Indonesian Airways said current market activity is very busy, especially on its flights through to Australia and New Zealand. There is also more demand from Indonesia for UK products such as general consumer goods and machine parts, she added.
After a slow summer, carriers operating to North America are seeing an upturn, BIFA's Blacklock said there is generally a September turnaround but business seems "to be generally up on last year."
The return of the winter schedules also means the market is not suffering from over-capacity on certain routes as the charters withdraw from the popular passenger destinations.

Average rates were marginally firmer at 62 pence a kg to JKF against 61 pence a fortnight ago, but stood at 70 pence to Los Angeles compared to 69 pence. Chicago's average was 68 pence, down from the previous 69 pence. A source from a Canadian airline said the London-Canada market has seen a pick-up after the holiday season. The Canadian market has been hit by low rates, like the U.S. market, he said.

The carrier was not looking to increase rates this autumn, he added, though they had fallen on last year's levels. He said many carriers are looking to April 1997 increases but he expressed scepticism about whether this month will be a good time to increase as there is again large amounts of capacity coming on to the market.
Much cargo is destined for the U.S.market, he added, and a lot of computer spares and car parts have been leaving the UK and Ireland for the U.S. market, he said.
Perhaps the most stable air cargo market - the Middle East - is steady. Average rates to Dubai were one pence higher at 71 pence but unchanged at 85 pence to Bahrain.
A Saudia source said the holiday season was very quiet as in the Middle East people attempt to escape the summer heat but currently it is very busy. Rates too are steady in this market.

Fawal Qarden of Royal Jordanian, said the market was doing fairly well, although not as good as last year. But within Europe, the UK was doing very well, with healthy demand for products such as machinery, books and educational materials.
Rates are remaining stable, he said and the carrier has no plans to increase its prices because of rising fuel prices.

Africa continues to generate much interest and one country many in the industry are talking about is Ethiopia. Alan Wise of the country's national carrier said Ethiopia is now a reasonable market and more money is being spent by the country he said.

Considerable exploration for minerals in being carried out , he added, and a lot of surveying equipment is going into Ethiopia. General consumer goods are being imported but it is not just one way traffic, he stressed. Exports include flowers, vegetables, spices, spice extracts and leather.
Latin America is another strong market and several large one-off cargo movements have taken place, industry sources said. Rates were steady around the 2.06 stg a kg level to Sao Paulo.
A gsa source, representing several Latin American carriers, said there is definitely more interest in Latin America.

Certainly with the companies involved in the North America market being hit by low rates, some carriers have become more "predatory" he said, "they are looking across the Atlantic where the rates are more healthy." Mexico has seen a recovery he said and rates to there are "respectable", he added. --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
